nodes.title: Integral primitive presentation with marked elements
nodes.statement: For every field L of characteristic zero, finitely generated over Q, and finite marked family s:I→L, there exist n≥0, a transcendence basis t:Fin n→L, a primitive element y, an injective evaluation j: A=Z[T₁,…,Tₙ]→L, its extension ĵ:F=Frac(A)→L, and H∈A[Y], with L=ĵ(F)(y), H(y,t)=0, deg_Y H>0, and H_F a nonzero scalar multiple of the monic minimal polynomial of y over F. Thus H_F is irreducible and separable. There are U_i∈A[Y] and V_i∈A\{0} with s_i=U_i(y,t)/V_i(t). One may choose deg_Y U_i<deg_Y H and a single common V for all i. A marked zero has numerator zero; the marked family is independent of any generating family.
hypotheses: Algebra.EssFiniteType Q L; I finite, possibly empty. Neither a presentation nor an embedding is assumed.
A has integer coefficients; the denominators V have no primitive-element variable. The equation H need not be monic.
proofSteps: Choose the finite transcendence basis and identify Q(t) with Frac(Q[T]) by aevalEquivField. Frac(Z[T]) and Frac(Q[T]) identify by their fraction-field universal properties: each rational coefficient is an integer divided by a nonzero integer. This identifies ĵ(F) with Q(t).

L is algebraic over Q(t) by the transcendence-basis property. A finite field-generating set for L over Q also generates over Q(t), so this algebraic extension is finite (finite_of_essFiniteType_of_isAlgebraic). Characteristic zero gives separability; choose y by the primitive-element theorem.

Use its power basis to write each s_i as a polynomial of degree below [L:F] in y. Clear the finite set of coefficients in F simultaneously by exist_integer_multiples. The denominator is in A, not in A[Y].

Integer-normalize the monic minimal polynomial to H. Its image is c times that polynomial with c≠0. Multiplication by c does not change degree, roots, irreducibility or separability over F. Transport the power-basis equalities through ĵ to obtain the marked identities.

sources.locator: Proof of Theorem I, (2), printed p.195
sources.match: The proof chooses independent parameters and a primitive element, then represents the finitely many marked elements using integral polynomials with parameter denominators.
The field is a finite simple extension of a rational function field; denominator clearing precedes specialization.

acceptance: L=Q permits n=0 and H=Y, y=0; s=1/6 has U=1,V=6.

No claim that an arbitrary finite set of marks generates L.

Apply the same integral presentation to nonzero marks and their inverses.
Includes all coefficients and an inverted nonzero element among the marks.

nodes.title: Transport through a primitive root
nodes.statement: Let A be a domain with F=Frac(A), let L/F be a finite simple extension generated by y, and let j:A→L be its scalar map. Suppose H∈A[Y] maps to C(c)·minpoly_F(y), c≠0. For any field E, injective e:A→E, and η∈E with H_e(η)=0, there is a unique ring homomorphism σ:L→E extending e on A and sending y to η. It is injective. Every marked identity x=U_j(y)/j(V) with V≠0 transports to σ(x)=U_e(η)/e(V).
hypotheses: The F-algebra structure on L is compatible with A; y is integral over F and F(y)=L.
E need not be algebraically closed. Irreducibility is over the embedded parameter field ê(F), not over E.
proofSteps: Extend e uniquely to ê:F→E by IsFractionRing.lift; the map is injective. Give E the F-algebra structure through ê.
Map H_F=C(c) minpoly to E. Since ê(c)≠0, the root equation implies minpoly_F(y) evaluated at η is zero.
Use algHomAdjoinIntegralEquiv (equivalently adjoinRootEquivAdjoin followed by root evaluation), then identify F(y) with L. The generator-value lemma gives σ(y)=η.

A field homomorphism is injective. Any other extension agrees on F by fraction-field uniqueness and on y; PowerBasis.algHom_ext proves uniqueness. Apply the homomorphism to every marked equality, using preservation of polynomial evaluation and division.

sources.locator: Theorem I proof, (10) and following paragraph, printed p.197
sources.match: Independent specialized parameters and a root of the primitive equation determine the whole-field embedding; the proof then transports the marked fractions.

acceptance: A root need not make H irreducible over E: for L=Q(√2) and E=Q₇ the selected root gives an embedding although H splits in E.
Without injectivity of e, the conclusion fails: sending a transcendence parameter to 0 does not extend to Q(t).
For a fixed root the extension is unique; different roots can give different embeddings.

nodes.title: Closure of the Lech integral embedding contract
nodes.statement: For L/Q finitely generated and every finite s⊂L, for each N there exist prime p>N and σ:L→Q_p with σ(s)⊂Z_p. This discharges the two presentation/transport obligations in the inherited lech-embedding-lemma; its endpoint and unit/localization corollaries retain their original ids.
hypotheses: The finite marked set may contain zero and may be empty.
No demand is made for every prime; the target is Q_p itself.
proofSteps: Apply integral-primitive-presentation to all marks and collect the finitely many nonzero parameter denominators.
Use the accepted lech-independent-hensel-specialization without changing its statement: it supplies ξ∈Z_pⁿ independent over Q, η∈Z_p satisfying H, and denominator units for arbitrarily large p.

The independent tuple makes parameter evaluation injective. Apply primitive-root-transport and its marked identity. Integral polynomial evaluation makes U(η,ξ) integral and each unit denominator has integral inverse.
For nonzero prescribed units, mark their inverses too; for the localized-adjoin corollary use the inherited ring-adjoin induction.

sources.match: Its integral intermediate conclusion is obtained before marking inverses yields units.
The prime-selection step has an elementary replacement; no Chebotarev input is needed.

acceptance: Q and the mark 1/6 require primes away from 2 and 3.
Q(√2) admits the example p=7, η≡3 mod7; p=3 does not work.
Zero has integral image and is not a unit.

nodes.title: Unramified Cohen coordinates with the coefficient map fixed
nodes.statement: Let R be a complete Noetherian regular local ring, char R=0, residue field F_p, with p∈m\m², dim R=g+1, and a fixed continuous local map Z_p→R inducing the identity on F_p. There is a continuous Z_p-algebra isomorphism R≃Z_p[[T₁,…,T_g]] carrying a chosen regular system (p,t₁,…,t_g) to (p,T₁,…,T_g). For a smooth relative-g-dimensional Z_p-scheme at an F_p-point this applies to its completed local ring.
hypotheses: The coefficient map is included and must be preserved; p∉m² is the unramified hypothesis.
g=0 is allowed; no such formula is asserted for ramified regular local rings.
proofSteps: Import the coefficient-ring existence and power-series surjection from SF.0/cohen-structure. Over F_p the unramified Cohen ring is Z_p.

A regular system extending p gives a surjection from the (p,T)-adically complete power-series ring. Both rings have dimension g+1; regularity makes the source a domain and forces the kernel to be zero.

Check compatibility with the specified Z_p map by continuity and density of Z. Smoothness supplies regularity, unramifiedness and the dimension of the completed local ring. This compatibility and completion adapter is requested explicitly from SF.0, not assumed to be part of its absolute statement.

sources.match: Uses an unramified complete regular local ring and a regular parameter system to obtain Z_p power-series coordinates.

acceptance: g=0 gives R≃Z_p.
Z_p[[T]] has dimension 2.
Z_p[π]/(π²−p), completed, is ramified and fails p∉m².

nodes.title: Call–Silverman specialization over a global height field and a curve
nodes.statement: Let K be a global height field with its chosen product-formula height structure, T/K a smooth projective geometrically integral curve, and h_T a nonnegative Weil height for a divisor of degree 1. Let V/K be smooth and projective and π:V→T a morphism with smooth geometrically integral generic fibre, P a rational section, and φ a rational self-map over T that is a morphism on the generic fibre. Let η∈Pic(V)⊗R and α>1, with φ*η−αη represented by a fibral divisor (supported over a proper closed subset of T), using the rational pullback convention of Call–Silverman §3. On a nonempty good open U where the fibres are smooth and geometrically integral and φ_t is a morphism, one has lim_{h_T(t)→∞, t∈U(K̄)} ĥ_{V_t,η_t,φ_t}(P_t)/h_T(t)=ĥ_{V_η,η_η,φ_η}(P_η). The right side uses the degree-normalized geometric height on K(T). The statement does not assert an O(1) error.
hypotheses: Use compatible height normalizations under finite extensions. The section is evaluated where defined. A projective model lets rational sections extend over the smooth curve.
A specified global height field is required; finite generation of K alone does not specify a height. Ampleness of η is not needed for the eigenclass limit.
proofSteps: The relative canonical/Weil-height difference is ≤C₁h_T(t)+C₂ by the general-curve version of Theorem 3.1; its constants are uniform in the point on the fibre.
For each fixed section Q=φⁿP, functoriality gives h_{V,η}(Q_t)=h_{T,Q*η}(t)+O_Q(1). Generic intersection degree equals the geometric Weil height of Q_η.

Use curve-height quasi-equivalence h_{T,D}(t)/h_T(t)→deg D, including real divisor classes; the height and intersection contracts are requested from RP.0. Combining with the generic canonical/Weil bound gives a limsup error bounded independently of Q after section-dependent O(1) terms vanish.

Replace P by φⁿP. Both canonical heights multiply by αⁿ. Divide the uniform limsup bound by αⁿ and let n tend to infinity. This generalizes the inherited t-line endpoint without requiring Northcott over K.

sources.locator: §3 Theorem 3.1 pp.177–182; §4 Theorem 4.1 and proof pp.183–186
sources.match: The proof compares fibre and generic heights along a section and amplifies by iteration on a smooth projective base curve.
The polynomial specialization proof needs this limit on a general base curve.

acceptance: T=P¹, K a number field and η=O(1) recover the inherited specialization theorem.

For the constant family f_t(z)=z² on P¹×P¹ over Q, the constant section P_t=2 has generic geometric height 0 and ratio h(2)/h(t)→0. The moving section P_t=t instead has generic height 1 and ratio h(t)/h(t)=1; a constant map alone does not force a zero limit.
A degree-e base change multiplies generic degrees and changes the degree-one base-height normalization accordingly.

nodes.title: Benedetto zero-height criterion for nonisotrivial polynomials
nodes.statement: Let F be any field, K/F a finite extension of F(T), and f∈K[z] a polynomial of degree d≥2 which is not affine-conjugate over a finite extension of K to a polynomial over the algebraic constant field. For every x∈P¹(K̄), its geometric canonical height is zero if and only if x is preperiodic.
hypotheses: The height uses geometric places trivial on F; this is not the number-field Northcott argument.
Isotriviality allows a finite extension and an affine change of coordinates.
proofSteps: Over any fixed finite extension containing x, zero local escape rates place its forward orbit in every local filled Julia set.

The rational zero-height set is forward-invariant. If it has at most two points it is already finite. Otherwise, if all places have potentially good reduction, normalize two finite zero-height points to 0 and 1; the product formula forces the leading coefficient to have norm 1 everywhere and then forces all coefficients to be constants (Benedetto Proposition 6.1). Nonisotriviality therefore supplies a bad place in this remaining case.

At a bad place the filled Julia set is covered by at most d² open discs of radius |a_d|^{-1/(d−1)}; at good places it lies in a closed disc of that radius. Two rational points in the same choices of bad-place discs violate the product formula. Thus the rational zero-height set is finite and forward-invariant.
Apply this argument in a finite extension containing any algebraic x. Nonisotriviality persists under that extension.

sources.locator: Theorems A–B p.2; Proposition 6.1 and proof of Theorem A pp.7–8
sources.match: Finiteness comes from local disc choices and a product-formula contradiction, with a separate constant-coefficient case.
The nonisotrivial branch of polynomial specialization uses this criterion.

acceptance: For f=z² over Q(T), x=2 has geometric height zero but is wandering: the exclusion is necessary.
f=z²+T and x=0 have positive geometric height.
Infinity is preperiodic for every polynomial and has height zero.

nodes.title: Disc covering at a place of bad polynomial reduction
nodes.statement: Over a complete algebraically closed nonarchimedean field, a polynomial f of degree d≥2 and leading coefficient a_d has filled Julia set contained in a unique smallest closed disc of radius r≥ρ=|a_d|^{-1/(d−1)}. Potential good reduction is equivalent to r=ρ. If r>ρ and z₀ is in the filled Julia set, that set is contained in the union of open discs D(x,ρ) for x∈f^{-2}(z₀), at most d² discs.
hypotheses: The absolute value is nonarchimedean and the field is complete and algebraically closed.
At potentially good places the containing disc is closed; at bad places the final covering discs are open.
proofSteps: The smallest-disc and inverse-disc theorems are the precise local input of Benedetto Lemmas 5.1–5.2. Their proofs are referenced there to the earlier local filled-Julia paper and remain a recorded gap.
For the covering conclusion, two inverse-image discs at distance r force in each fibre at least one second preimage at distance ≥r from a point outside all open radius-ρ discs.
Factor f(z)−y and then f²(z)−z₀. The product bounds imply |f²(z)−z₀|>r for such a point, excluding it from the filled Julia set (Lemma 5.3).

sources.match: The first two statements are cited local results; the last is proved by factoring the two inverse-image levels.

acceptance: For z^d, the filled Julia set is the closed unit disc and r=ρ=1.
Replacing open discs by closed ones at a bad place destroys the strict product-formula inequality.

nodes.title: Legendre marked-point degree growth
nodes.statement: For c∈C(t)∪{∞} other than 0,1,t,∞, write its primitive homogeneous lift C and put F₁=F(C)/gcd(F(C)), d=deg F₁. Then d≥2; if F₁=(P₁,Q₁), P₁(0,1)P₁(1,0)≠0, Q₁(1,0)=0 and P₁(1,1)≠Q₁(1,1). Recursively F_{n+1}=F(F_n)/t₂² has nonzero resultant and degree 4ⁿd. Consequently c is not preperiodic over C(t), and the only persistently preperiodic rational marks are 0,1,t,∞.
hypotheses: F=( (t₁w²−t₂z²)², 4t₂zw(w−z)(t₁w−t₂z) ); n≥1.
Degree is degree in the parameter after removal of the common homogeneous factor.
proofSteps: Separate constant marks, the scaled c=t times a constant case, and general lifts A=t₁^l A′, B=t₂^k B′. The only possible common factors arise at t₁,t₂,t₁−t₂ because noncusp fibres define morphisms. Compute their orders.
After the first cancellation the boundary values above hold; at t₁=t₂ with A=B use the first-order expansion to see P₁−Q₁ does not vanish after cancellation.
These conditions force exactly t₂² cancellation in the next step, preserve the boundary values, and make its degree quadruple. Unbounded parameter degree excludes equality of two iterates.

For the four excluded marks the explicit formula gives eventual arrival at infinity. Restricting to constant marks removes the moving mark t, yielding the inherited common-to-all torsion-image target.

sources.locator: Proposition 3.1 and proof pp.9–10; §3.2 p.10; Proposition 1.4 p.3
sources.match: The degree calculation includes rational moving marks; the common constant torsion images are its constant-mark consequence.

acceptance: c=2 gives initial degree 2.
c=t is a persistent torsion mark but is not a constant common image.
The exclusions include infinity, not just the finite branch coordinates.

nodes.title: Continuous marked escape potential across the three Legendre cusps
nodes.statement: For c∈C(t) other than 0,1,t, choose the primitive homogeneous lift C, the cancelled F₁ and F_{n+1} of legendre-marked-degree-growth, with d=deg F₁. The functions (d·4^{n−1})^{-1} log max(|P_n|,|Q_n|) converge locally uniformly on C² minus the origin to a continuous plurisubharmonic function G_C. It satisfies G_C(λt)=G_C(t)+log|λ|. Its projective curvature defines a probability bifurcation measure μ_c; continuity at the cusp parameters 0,1,infinity prevents this probability from being supported only at those cusps.
hypotheses: A finite rational mark, including nonconstant marks, is allowed. Use the primitive cancellation and degree normalization from the preceding target.
Local uniform convergence includes nonzero homogeneous parameter vectors representing the three singular fibres.
proofSteps: Away from the cusps, nonvanishing of the resultant gives the usual summable successive escape-rate estimate.

DWY §4 separates the estimates at infinity, zero, and one; its Proposition 4.1 identifies the boundary limits through the nonzero boundary values from degree growth. These cusp-uniform estimates remain a named proof leaf, rather than being inferred from the nondegenerate estimate.
Each normalized function is plurisubharmonic and logarithmically homogeneous of degree one. Local uniform convergence preserves continuity, plurisubharmonicity and the logarithmic scaling relation.

The projective curvature has total mass one. A continuous local potential has no point atoms, so the measure has nonzero mass on the nonsingular parameter domain. This supplies the nontrivial activity measure used in §6.5.

sources.match: The convergence extends across all three cusps, not just the good parameter domain.

acceptance: The logarithmic scaling coefficient is 1 after degree normalization, not d.
The good-parameter resultant estimate alone does not prove uniform convergence at a cusp.

nodes.title: Infinitely many torsion specializations of a constant Legendre mark
nodes.statement: For a∈Q̄\{0,1}, there are infinitely many distinct t∈Q̄\{0,1} for which a is preperiodic for f_t, equivalently either point of E_t over x=a is torsion.
hypotheses: Infinity is handled separately as a persistent mark. The choice of sign of the point does not affect torsion.
proofSteps: The marked degree growth implies a nonzero activity/bifurcation measure, by the convergence of normalized marked escape rates in DWY Theorem 1.5.

DWY §6.5 invokes the normal-family criterion and a Montel argument: an active mark in the Legendre family has infinitely many preperiodic parameters. This analytic bridge, rather than the entire equivalence in Theorem 1.2, is the remaining gap recorded here.

Each preperiodic relation is an algebraic equation over Q̄ in t. It is not identically zero by marked degree growth; its roots are algebraic. The inherited semiconjugacy identifies them with torsion parameters.

sources.match: The proof establishes infinitude of Tor(c) by non-normality before using equidistribution for the equivalence theorem.

acceptance: Do not infer infinitude just by writing more division polynomials: distinct roots still need proof.
The mark a=0 is torsion for every good parameter and belongs to the separate persistent case.

nodes.title: Uniform hybrid escape potentials for meromorphic families
nodes.statement: Let f_t be a degree-d≥2 meromorphic family of morphisms of P¹ on a punctured disc, with meromorphic homogeneous lift F_t having no common zero for t≠0. Fix 0<r<1 inside the parameter disc and the hybrid central norm |T|=r. With the Fubini–Study reference metric define u_n([z],t)=d^{-n} log(max_i |(F_t^n(z))_i| / ||z||₂^{d^n}), where F_t^n is the homogeneous compositional iterate. The finite-level hybrid extensions of (log r/log|t|)u_n converge uniformly over the closed hybrid disc |t|≤r to a continuous potential. Its central restriction is g_F([z])=lim_n d^{-n}log||F^n(z)||_sup−log||z||_sup over C((T)) with |T|=r, relative to the standard nonarchimedean model metric. Replacing F_t by h(t)F_t changes the limit by (log r/log|t|)log|h(t)|/(d−1) on complex fibres and by log|h|_r/(d−1) centrally.
hypotheses: The resultant may vanish at t=0 but not for t≠0; the family is meromorphic across 0.

Use the Fubini–Study metric on complex O(1) and the standard model metric centrally. Scalar changes of the homogeneous lift use the displayed correction; continuity is stronger information than weak convergence of measures.
proofSteps: Coefficient meromorphy gives an upper bound by a power of |t|; a Nullstellensatz/resultant identity gives the lower bound by another power. Thus |u_{n+1}−u_n|≤C d^{-n}log|t|^{-1} (Favre Proposition 4.4).
The hybrid scaling converts the estimate to a summable bound independent of the parameter. Finite-level model potentials extend continuously to the central fibre by Theorem 2.10.

Uniform convergence proves continuity and identifies the central escape potential by evaluation of the same iterated homogeneous polynomials. The hybrid model-function extension is requested from TB.0.

sources.locator: Theorem 2.10 p.15; §4.3 Proposition 4.4 and central-potential identification pp.29–31
sources.match: A meromorphic growth estimate for successive normalized potentials produces the uniform potential in the hybrid setting.

acceptance: A constant lift with good reduction has central potential g_F=0 for the standard model metric.
Unscaled complex potentials are not asserted continuous at t=0.

nodes.title: Hybrid limit of equilibrium measures
nodes.statement: For the family and normalization of hybrid-uniform-potential, the complex equilibrium probabilities μ_t, embedded in their hybrid fibres, converge weakly as t→0 to the nonarchimedean equilibrium probability μ_f on the central fibre: every continuous hybrid test function has convergent integral.
hypotheses: Weak convergence is in the hybrid space, not ordinary weak convergence on a fixed complex sphere.
proofSteps: The finite-level model-function measures have convergent test integrals across the hybrid fibres.

Use the uniform potential convergence and the continuity of the Monge–Ampère/Laplacian measure operation under uniform admissible-potential approximation (Favre Theorem 4.2). The model-function density of Theorem 2.12 extends convergence to all continuous test functions.

Identify the complex measure as maximal entropy and the central measure as the nonarchimedean equilibrium measure. For the Legendre family use the inherited explicit central measure and its cusp segment to obtain annular masses.

sources.locator: Theorem B p.3; Theorems 2.12 and 4.2; §4.3 proof pp.30–31

nodes.title: Finite multiplier spectra off the Lattès locus
nodes.statement: For each degree d≥2, finitely many iterated fixed-point multiplier multisets jointly define a morphism on M_d with finite fibres on the non-Lattès locus. Equivalently one may take a sufficiently divisible single iterate N, depending only on d, whose fixed-point multiplier spectrum has finite fibres there.
hypotheses: Exclude all affine-torus Lattès maps for this finiteness input. Flexible-only exclusion is obtained using the separate rigid finiteness target.
Multipliers at fixed points of an iterate include multiplicity.
proofSteps: McMullen Corollary 2.3 says the full sequence of multiplier spectra determines a nonaffine conjugacy class up to finitely many choices. Its proof rests on stable-family rigidity, Theorem 2.2.

Noetherianity of the algebraic equal-spectrum loci gives a finite set of spectra sufficient to have zero-dimensional fibres outside the Lattès locus. A sufficiently divisible iterate packages them; check the finite ambiguity of taking roots and accounting for exact periods.
The stable-family rigidity and the finite truncation/iterate adapter are recorded as gaps; Ingram Lemma 14 is the verified downstream use.

sources.match: The multiplier spectrum detects nonaffine algebraic deformations.
Uses a finite-fibre iterated spectrum to compare an ample moduli height.

acceptance: Flexible Lattès families have constant spectra and positive-dimensional moduli, so their removal is necessary.
The number of iterates depends on d; no universal single period is claimed.

nodes.title: Affine-torus Lattès maps
nodes.statement: A complex rational map f of degree ≥2 is an affine-torus Lattès map if there exist a rank-two lattice Λ⊂C, the torus T=C/Λ, an affine endomorphism L(z)=az+b with aΛ⊂Λ and |a|²>1, and a finite holomorphic quotient Θ:T→P¹ such that f∘Θ=Θ∘L. The classification normalizes Θ to T/G_n for n∈{2,3,4,6}, with ω_nΛ=Λ and (1−ω_n)b∈Λ. Flexibility is equivalent to n=2 and a an integer.
hypotheses: Λ has rank two; cylinder quotients give power/Chebyshev maps and are excluded.
Finite quotient is essential. The translation b is allowed; the inherited multiplication-only Lattès map is a special case.
proofSteps: Use the quotient-of-affine-map notion of Milnor Definition 2.1 restricted to a torus. The semiconjugacy determines degree |a|².
Milnor Theorem 3.1 and Lemma 3.5 give the cyclic quotient normal form; Theorem 5.1 fixes the conjugacy invariants.

Lemma 5.5 identifies flexibility. Elliptic uniformization and the cyclic-quotient classification remain a precise recorded gap; do not identify the whole notion with inherited multiplication-only maps.

sources.locator: Definition 2.1 pp.2–3; Theorem 3.1 pp.3–4 and Lemma 3.5 pp.5–6; Theorem 5.1 pp.15–16; Lemma 5.5 p.18
sources.match: The affine torus quotient includes rigid maps and translations as well as the flexible multiplication cases.

acceptance: All inherited multiplication-by-m examples are included.
z↦z^d is a cylinder quotient and is not a torus quotient.

uses.how: Separates the finitely many rigid classes from flexible families.
Justifies replacement of the full exceptional locus by the flexible locus.

nodes.title: Finiteness of rigid Lattès classes in fixed degree
nodes.statement: For each d≥2, there are finitely many complex affine-torus Lattès conjugacy classes of degree d which are not flexible. The classes defined over Q̄ therefore have bounded ample moduli height.
hypotheses: Conjugacy classes are counted, not presentations or rational maps with chosen coordinates.
The bounded-height assertion is only on algebraic classes.
proofSteps: If n≥3, normalize Λ to the Gaussian or Eisenstein lattice and use |a|²=d; only finitely many a and translation quotient invariants occur.
For n=2, nonflexibility forces a∉Z. Its equation is a²−qa+d=0 with q²<4d, leaving finitely many a. Milnor Lemma 5.4 bounds the normalized lattice shapes for each a by writing a=r+sγ and Im γ≥√3/2.
Theorem 5.1 leaves only a finite translation quotient for each fixed lattice and a. Thus only finitely many rigid classes occur, and any height is bounded on the finite algebraic subset.

sources.match: The invariants and the lattice bound yield fixed-degree finiteness of the rigid classes.

acceptance: Degree 2 has rigid examples.
Degree 4 also has a flexible family, so finiteness of all Lattès classes is false.

nodes.title: Minimum conjugate coefficient height versus moduli height
nodes.statement: For each d≥2 and a fixed ample height h_M on a projective compactification of M_d/Q̄, there are c₁,c₂>0 and C₁,C₂ with c₁h_M([f])−C₁≤inf_{g conjugate to f}h_Hom(g)≤c₂h_M([f])+C₂. A representative attaining the bound up to a fixed additive constant suffices; no attainment of the infimum is required for subsequent inequalities.
hypotheses: Absolute coefficient heights and algebraic Möbius conjugacy; constants depend on d and the height choices, not f.
proofSteps: The quotient morphism and the height machine give the direction bounding h_M by coefficient height.

The reverse direction requires a bounded-height choice of representative in every conjugacy class. Ingram Lemma 13 cites Silverman, Moduli Spaces and Arithmetic Dynamics (2012), p.103; its proof was not located in a public or cleared source and remains the recorded gap.
Use the infimum form, or choose a representative within 1 of it, in the critical-height argument. This avoids relying on attainment of an absolute-height minimum over all of Q̄.

sources.match: The coefficient-height error is replaced by a bound depending on the moduli class.

acceptance: Conjugating a fixed map by large-height Möbius maps can make its raw coefficient height arbitrarily large.
A single arbitrary representative cannot replace the infimum.

nodes.title: Height comparison on the whole finite-fibre locus
nodes.statement: Let X,Y be irreducible projective varieties over Q̄ with ample line bundles A,B, U⊂X open, and F:U→Y a morphism with finite fibres. There exist C>0,D with h_A(u)≤C h_B(F(u))+D for every algebraic u∈U.
hypotheses: The map is defined on U only; the inequality includes every point of U.
proofSteps: Replace Y by the closure of F(U); the map is generically finite. RP.0/silverman-dominant-map-inequality supplies the bound away from a proper closed subset Z of X.
On each irreducible component of Z meeting U, restrict the ample bundles and the finite-fibre map. Induct on dimension, using its image closure as the new target.
There are finitely many components. After lower-bounding the ample target height, adjust constants and take maxima to obtain one bound on all of U.

sources.match: Induction extends a generically finite height comparison from a dense open to the entire finite-fibre locus.

acceptance: A constant morphism from a positive-dimensional U has infinite fibres and fails the hypothesis.
The proof must treat the exceptional closed subset; the dense-open supplier alone does not give the conclusion.

nodes.title: Quantitative branch point near a small attracting multiplier
nodes.statement: Let f(z)=λz·∏_{i=1}^{d−1}(1−α_i z)/∏_{j=1}^{d−1}(1−β_j z) have degree d≥2, fixing 0 and infinity, and M=max{|α_i|,|β_j|}>0. Over C set C_v=3^{d−1}, ε_v=min(1/8,1/C_v); over a complete algebraically closed nonarchimedean field of characteristic 0 or p>d set C_v=1, ε_v=min_{1≤m≤d}|m|^d. If 0<|λ|<ε_v, there is a nonzero branch value β with 0<|f^k(β)|M≤(C_v|λ|)^k for all k≥1.
hypotheses: The archimedean absolute value is the usual complex modulus. In the nonarchimedean case the field characteristic is 0 or p>d, as in Ingram §1; the residue characteristic can be at most d.
A branch value is the image of a critical point, not necessarily the critical point itself.
proofSteps: Rescale so M=1. On the half-unit disc over C, or the open unit disc nonarchimedean, the displayed factorization bounds iterates by a geometric power and excludes hitting 0.

Over C, if the relevant disc has no branch value, the inverse component maps unbranched to it. Koebe quarter bounds its conformal radius by 4 because a pole or nonzero root lies on the unit circle, whereas the multiplier gives radius 1/(2|λ|), a contradiction.

Nonarchimedean: the Benedetto–Ingram–Jones–Levy theorem used in Ingram Lemma 8 yields a branch value in the unit disc if |λ| is below every directional multiplicity to the dth power. Those multiplicities lie between 1 and d, giving the stated ε_v. These two analytic suppliers remain explicit gaps.

sources.locator: §1 field convention p.4; Lemma 8 and proofs pp.7–8
sources.match: Uses Koebe quarter in the complex case and the small-residue-prime directional-multiplicity bound in the nonarchimedean case.

acceptance: For residue characteristic p>d, ε_v=1.
For small p the threshold cannot be replaced by 1.
The result does not cover a superattracting multiplier λ=0.

nodes.title: Equal-degree Bilu–Tichy classification input
nodes.statement: If K is a number field, S a finite set of nonarchimedean places, F,G∈K[X] have equal degree >1 and F(x)=G(y) has infinitely many S-integral solutions, then F=E∘F₁∘a and G=E∘G₁∘b for E∈K[X] and affine a,b∈K[X], where, up to interchanging F₁,G₁, the pair is (X,X), (X²,c∘X²) with affine c, (D₂(X,α)/α,D₂(X,β)/β) with nonzero α,β∈K, or (D_n(X,α),−D_n(X cos(π/n),α)) with α∈K and cos(2π/n)∈K. D_n is the Dickson polynomial characterized by D_n(U+V,UV)=Uⁿ+Vⁿ.
hypotheses: n is a positive integer, parameters are interpreted in a chosen algebraic closure in the fourth case. Only the equal-degree necessity is needed.
proofSteps: Siegel bounds the genus and number of points at infinity of a component with infinitely many S-integral points.
Bilu–Tichy classify the resulting genus-zero polynomial pairs through polynomial decomposition. This classification proof is not given in GTZ and is retained as a precise gap.

For the downstream shape corollary, normalize nonzero Dickson parameters by a square root over K̄. Up to affine composition, a common H is Xⁿ or D_n(X,1); the cyclotomic degree bound makes the admissible n finite for fixed K.

sources.match: States the equal-degree classification and proves the affine-normalized finite list of shared shapes.

acceptance: For F=G take E=F and (F₁,G₁)=(X,X).
Infinitely many complex solutions alone give no arithmetic classification.

nodes.title: Ritt classification for equal common iterates
nodes.statement: For F,G∈C[X], deg F=d>1 and a positive integer n, F^{∘n}=G^{∘n} iff there exist β∈C, γ∈C× and H∈X^r C[X^s] (r,s≥0) such that F(X)=−β+γH(X+β), G(X)=−β+H(X+β), γ^s=1 and γ^{1+d+⋯+d^{n−1}}=1. If s=0 then X^r C[X^s] consists of scalar multiples of X^r.
hypotheses: n≥1. Iterate composition is distinct from ordinary polynomial powers.
proofSteps: The backward implication is a direct composition calculation using H(γX)=γ^rH(X) and d≡r modulo s when s>0; for a monomial use d=r.
The forward implication is the Ritt classification cited as GTZ Proposition 6.3; its proof remains a gap.

For coefficients in a characteristic-zero field K, γ is the ratio of leading coefficients and belongs to K. Its order m is coprime to d. Prime-power multiplicative orders give a common-iterate exponent ≤m, yielding the bounded-root-of-unity corollary used in GTZ Proposition 6.1.

sources.locator: Proposition 6.3 and Corollary 6.4 with proof, p.17
sources.match: Records the equal-iterate classification and proves the uniform exponent consequence.

acceptance: n=1 forces γ=1.
F=−X²,G=X² have no equal positive iterate: d=2 and γ=−1 violate the geometric-sum condition.
F=−X³,G=X³ agree at the second iterate.

nodes.title: Common iterates from synchronized affine intersections
nodes.statement: Let K have characteristic zero, f(X)=aX+b and g(X)=cX+e with a,c nonzero. If the set of common values fⁿ(x₀)=gⁿ(y₀), with the same n≥0, is infinite, then f^{∘m}=g^{∘m} for some m≥1. Together with conjugating a nonvertical line to the diagonal, this supplies the linear case of the inherited polynomial-lines DML target.
hypotheses: Infinitude concerns distinct common values, not merely infinitely many time indices. Both slopes are nonzero; constant maps have finite synchronized image.
proofSteps: Reduce to the finitely generated characteristic-zero subfield containing the coefficients and initial points, embed it in C, and shift to a first common value. A nontrivial root-of-unity slope has a finite orbit and is excluded by distinct-value infinitude.

If both slopes differ from 1, write the two iterates using their fixed-point translations. If the translated starting values differ, their equality becomes A aⁿ+B cⁿ=1 with A,B nonzero. The finitely generated multiplicative subgroup generated by a,c meets the exact DT.2 two-variable unit-equation contract; distinct n give distinct solutions because a is not a root of unity. Thus the translated starting values coincide, forcing equal fixed points and aⁿ=cⁿ at a return, hence equality of the corresponding affine iterates.

If both slopes are 1, equality after shifting to a common start forces the two translation increments to coincide. If exactly one slope is 1, the nontrivial translation grows linearly along the common-return subsequence. A slope of complex modulus at most 1 gives a bounded other orbit; one of modulus greater than 1 grows exponentially. Either contradicts infinitely many returns (GTZ Proposition 5.3).

GTZ Lemma 5.1 handles nonvertical lines by affine conjugation; a vertical or horizontal line with infinitely many distinct orbit points is periodic because the relevant coordinate is periodic. Use the inherited finite-union-of-progressions contract for time sets.

sources.locator: §5 Lemma 5.1 and Proposition 5.3 with proof, pp.12–13
sources.match: The synchronized linear case is proved separately; the two-variable unit equation supplies the arithmetic finiteness input.

acceptance: f=g=X+1 has infinitely many synchronized common values from a common initial point.
Two identity maps can meet at every time but at only one value; the theorem does not infer line periodicity from that finite image.
Independent-time intersections differ: X+1 and X² can have infinite orbit intersection without a common iterate.
